t.6.80.1: Then the ministers of Paulastya, having heard that Indrajit was slain and having ascertained it, anguished, reported it to Daśagrīva.
t.6.80.2: O great king, O greatly splendid one, your son has been slain in battle by Lakṣmaṇa, aided by Vibhīṣaṇa, while we looked on.
t.6.80.4: Having heard of that frightful, cruel and terrible slaying of his son Indrajit in battle, he fell into a great swoon.
t.6.80.3: O wise one, your son Indrajit, a hero never defeated in battles, has met another hero in combat and been slain by the valiant Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.80.5: Regaining consciousness after a long while, the king, foremost of the Rākṣasas, afflicted by grief for his son, wretched and with his senses in turmoil, lamented.
t.6.80.6: Alas, O chief of the rākṣasa army, my child, great chariot-warrior! Having conquered Indra, how is it that today you have fallen into the power of Lakṣmaṇa?
t.6.80.7: Surely, when enraged, you could pierce with your arrows even Kāla and Antaka, and even the peaks of Mandara; how much more, then, Lakṣmaṇa in battle!
t.6.80.8: Today King Vaivasvata is held in even greater esteem by me, he by whom you, O mighty-armed one, have today been united with the law of time.
t.6.80.9: This is the path of good warriors, honored even among all the hosts of the immortals: the man who is slain for the sake of his master attains heaven.
t.6.80.10: Today all the hosts of gods, the guardians of the worlds, and the seers as well, seeing Indrajit slain, will sleep in comfort, free from fear.
t.6.80.11: Today the three worlds in their entirety, and the earth with its forests, bereft of Indrajit alone, seem to me as though empty.
t.6.80.12: Today I shall hear in the inner apartments the wailing of the daughters of the Nairṛtas, like the trumpeting of a herd of she-elephants in a mountain cave.
t.6.80.13: O scorcher of foes, where have you gone, abandoning us: the office of crown prince, Laṅkā, the rākṣasas, your mother, me, and your wife?
t.6.80.14: O hero, it is you who must perform my funeral rites once I have gone to the abode of Yama, for you are set on a perverse course.
t.6.80.16: As Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, lay stricken, lamenting in these and other such words, a mighty rage born of the calamity that had befallen his son took possession of him.
t.6.80.15: While Sugrīva lives, and Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, where have you gone, abandoning us, without drawing out the thorn that pierces me?
t.6.80.17: That form of his, terrible by nature, now inflamed by the fire of wrath, became unapproachable, like the form of Rudra when enraged.
t.6.80.19: As he gnashed his teeth, the sound of his grinding was heard, like that of a great machine being wound up by the Dānavas.
t.6.80.18: From the eyes of that enraged one teardrops fell, like drops of oil, still bearing flame, falling from two blazing lamps.
t.6.80.20: Enraged like the fire of time at the end of the world, in whatever direction he looked, in that very direction the rākṣasas, stricken with fear, hid themselves.
t.6.80.21: The rākṣasas did not approach him as he gazed in all directions, enraged like Antaka, the Ender, eager to devour all things moving and unmoving.
t.6.80.22: Then Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, filled with the utmost rage, spoke in the midst of the rākṣasas, wishing to make them stand firm in battle.
t.6.80.23: Having practiced austerities hard to perform for thousands of years in those various places, I pleased Svayambhū, the Self-born.
t.6.80.24: By the fruition of that very austerity and by the grace of Svayambhū, I never have any fear from the asuras, nor from the devas.
t.6.80.25: My armour, given by Brahmā, which shines with a splendour equal to the sun's, was not pierced by thunderbolts and spears in the battles between the gods and the asuras.
t.6.80.26: Today, when I am furnished with that and stand in my chariot here in the battle, who could face me in the fight today, even Puraṃdara himself in person?
t.6.80.27: That great bow, together with its arrows, which Svayambhū, well pleased, gave to me then during the clashes between the devas and the asuras.
t.6.80.28: Today let the great and terrible bow be raised up to the sound of hundreds of trumpets, for the slaying of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the supreme battle.
t.6.80.29: Tormented by the slaying of his son, the valiant Rāvaṇa fell under the sway of rage, and, having deliberated in his mind, he resolved to kill Sītā.
t.6.80.31: Through illusion, in order to deceive the forest-dwellers, my child slew something there and displayed it, saying, "This is Sītā."
t.6.80.30: Then the copper-eyed one, exceedingly dreadful yet dejected, looked around at all those night-roaming rākṣasas, fearsome to behold and speaking in dejected voices, and addressed them.
t.6.80.32: "I shall make this come true and do what is pleasing to myself: I shall destroy Vaidehī, who is devoted to that wretch of a kṣatriya." Having spoken thus to his ministers, he quickly seized his sword.
t.6.80.33: Drawing out his sword, rich in fine qualities and gleaming like the clear sky, he rushed forth swiftly from the assembly hall, surrounded by his ministers.
t.6.80.34: Rāvaṇa, his mind deeply distraught with grief for his son, seized a sword in fury and rushed at once to where Maithilī was.
t.6.80.35: Seeing the rākṣasa setting out, they raised a lion's roar; and seeing him enraged, the rākṣasas embraced one another and spoke.
t.6.80.36: Today, on seeing him, those two brothers will be struck with dread, for the four guardians of the worlds were conquered by him in his wrath, and many other foes were struck down in battles.
t.6.80.37: While they were talking among themselves, Rāvaṇa, overwhelmed with rage, rushed toward Vaidehī, who had gone to the Aśoka grove.
t.6.80.38: Though held back by his well-meaning friends, he, enraged beyond measure, rushed forward in fury, like a malignant planet in the sky rushing upon Rohiṇī.
t.6.80.39: But the blameless Maithilī, guarded by the rākṣasa women, saw the enraged rākṣasa bearing an excellent sword.
t.6.80.40: Seeing him sword in hand, refusing to turn back though his friends tried again and again to restrain him, the daughter of Janaka was stricken with distress.
t.6.80.41: Since this evil-minded one, enraged, is rushing at me himself, he will kill me as though I were helpless, though I have a protector.
t.6.80.42: Again and again he urged me, though I was devoted to my husband, saying, “Become my wife and take your pleasure,” but he was rejected by me.
t.6.80.43: This one, plainly driven to despair because I would not yield to him, is now possessed by anger and delusion and has risen up to kill me.
t.6.80.44: Or else those two tigers among men, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have today been struck down in battle by that ignoble one on my account. Alas, shame! This destruction of the two princes has come about because of me.
t.6.80.45: Indeed, that advice of Hanūmān was not followed by me, wretched as I am; had I then gone away on his back, blameless, I would not now be grieving thus, for I would be resting in my husband's lap.
t.6.80.46: But I think the heart of that Kausalyā will burst when she, who has only one son, hears that her son has perished in battle.
t.6.80.47: For she, weeping, will call to mind the birth, the childhood and the youth of that great-souled one, his righteous deeds and his handsome form.
t.6.80.48: Her son slain, bereft of hope and senseless with grief, she will surely offer the funeral rites and then mount the fire, or else she will enter the waters.
t.6.80.49: Shame upon the wicked hunchback Mantharā, of sinful intent, on whose account Kausalyā shall undergo this sorrow!
t.6.80.50: Seeing Maithilī, the wretched one, lamenting thus, like Rohiṇī who, parted from the Moon, has fallen into the power of a malign planet,
t.6.80.51: A wise minister named Supārśva spoke these words to Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, as he was being restrained by his counselors.
t.6.80.52: O Daśagrīva, you who are the very younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa, how is it that, casting aside dharma in your anger, you wish to kill Vaidehī?
t.6.80.53: You have completed the vows of Vedic learning and are ever devoted to your own dharma; why then, O hero, lord of the rākṣasas, do you think of killing a woman?
t.6.80.54: Look upon Maithilī, endowed with beauty, O king, and you yourself, together with us, let go of your anger toward Rāghava.
t.6.80.56: Valiant and wise, a chariot-warrior armed with a sword, mounted upon the finest of chariots, you shall slay Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and win Maithilī.
t.6.80.55: Make your preparations this very day, the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, and then, surrounded by your forces, march out for victory on the day of the new moon.
t.6.80.57: That evil-minded Rāvaṇa, having accepted the most righteous words spoken by his friend, then went to his palace; and thereafter the mighty one, surrounded by his friends, again proceeded to the assembly hall.
